Abductor pollicis longus: Moves the thumb away from the hand and helps tilt the wrist toward the thumb.
Minor role; keeps the hand relaxed and steady during the arm swing.
De Quervain's tendon irritation from repetitive gripping.
Adductor brevis: Pulls the thigh in toward the midline and helps flex the hip.
Stops the knee drifting outward and steadies the pelvis in stance.
Groin strain with sudden sideways moves or sprinting.
Adductor longus: Pulls the thigh in toward the midline and helps flex the hip.
Controls the leg's line under the body; works hard when speeding up.
The most commonly strained groin muscle.
Adductor magnus & minimus: Pulls the thigh in and, with its back part, extends the hip.
Helps push the body forward and keeps the knee tracking straight.
Anconeus: Helps straighten the elbow and steadies the joint.
Small helper to the triceps in the backward arm swing.
Rarely injured; can be sore with elbow overuse.
Anterior cruciate ligament: Stops the shin sliding forward under the thigh and limits knee rotation.
Keeps the knee stable on landing and when changing direction.
ACL tears from pivoting, cutting or landing on a straight, inward-collapsing knee.
Articularis genus: Lifts the knee joint capsule when the knee straightens.
Keeps the capsule from being pinched as the knee extends with each stride.
Biceps brachii: Bends the elbow and turns the palm up.
Holds the elbow bent at about 90 degrees for an efficient arm swing.
Tightness if the arms are carried too high or clenched.
Biceps femoris (long head): Bends the knee and extends the hip.
Slows the swinging leg before foot strike and drives the hip back in push-off.
Hamstring strain, most often in sprinting at late swing.
Biceps femoris (short head): Bends the knee and turns the shin outward.
Controls knee extension in late swing.
Brachialis: Keeps the elbow angle steady in the arm swing.
Strain is uncommon; soreness with overuse.
Brachioradialis: Bends the elbow, strongest with the thumb pointing up.
Helps hold the bent-elbow arm position.
Forearm tightness from gripping or clenched fists.
Coracobrachialis: Brings the arm forward and in toward the body.
Rarely injured; sore with heavy overhead work.
Deltoid (anterior): Drives the forward part of the arm swing.
Shoulder strain or impingement from overuse.
Deltoid (middle): Raises the arm out to the side.
Steadies the shoulder; shouldn't lift the arms away from the body.
Deltoid (posterior): Drives the backward part of the arm swing.
Extensor carpi radialis brevis: Extends the wrist and tilts it toward the thumb.
Keeps the wrist neutral and relaxed.
Extensor carpi radialis longus: Extends the wrist and tilts it toward the thumb.
Extensor carpi ulnaris: Extends the wrist and tilts it toward the little finger.
Wrist stability during the arm swing.
Tendon irritation on the little-finger side of the wrist.
Extensor digitorum: Straightens the fingers and helps extend the wrist.
Keeps the hand relaxed rather than clenched.
Extensor digitorum longus: Lifts the toes and the front of the foot.
Clears the toes off the ground in the swing phase.
Shin splints and tendon irritation on top of the foot (tight laces).
Extensor hallucis longus: Lifts the big toe and helps lift the foot.
Clears the big toe in swing.
Tendon irritation on top of the foot.
Extensor pollicis brevis: Straightens the thumb at its base.
Fibularis brevis: Turns the sole outward and points the foot.
Steadies the ankle against rolling over on uneven ground.
Tendon irritation behind the outer ankle; weak after ankle sprains.
Fibularis longus: Turns the sole outward, points the foot and supports the arch.
Stabilises the ankle and arch at foot strike and push-off.
Peroneal tendon pain; ankle instability after sprains.
Fibularis tertius: Lifts the foot and turns the sole outward.
Helps clear the foot in swing.
Flexor carpi radialis: Bends the wrist and tilts it toward the thumb.
Flexor carpi ulnaris: Bends the wrist and tilts it toward the little finger.
Flexor digitorum longus: Curls the four small toes and points the foot.
Helps the toes grip and push off; supports the arch.
Flexor digitorum profundus: Shouldn't be working hard: clenched fists add tension.
Flexor hallucis longus: Curls the big toe and points the foot.
Powers the final push-off through the big toe.
Tendon pain behind the inner ankle.
Gastrocnemius: Points the foot and helps bend the knee.
Main push-off power with every stride; absorbs load at foot strike.
Gluteus maximus: Extends and externally rotates the hip.
Main power for push-off and climbing; keeps the trunk upright.
Weak glutes overload the hamstrings, back and knees.
Gluteus medius: Moves the leg out to the side and keeps the pelvis level.
Stops the hip dropping on the swing side in single-leg stance.
Weakness linked to runner's knee and IT band pain.
Gluteus minimus: Moves the leg out and rotates it inward; keeps the pelvis level.
Works with gluteus medius in stance.
Gracilis: Pulls the thigh in and bends the knee.
Iliacus: Tight hip flexors tilt the pelvis forward and strain the low back.
Iliotibial tract: A thick band of fascia that steadies the outer hip and knee.
Tensioned by the gluteus maximus and TFL to stabilise the knee.
IT band syndrome: pain on the outer knee.
Infraspinatus: Rotates the arm outward; rotator cuff.
Keeps the shoulder joint centred during the arm swing.
Interosseous membrane: Connects the paired forearm / lower-leg bones and spreads load between them.
Transfers force between tibia and fibula on landing.
Can be involved in shin splints.
Lateral collateral ligament: Stops the knee opening on its outer side.
Sprain from a blow to the inner knee.
Lateral patellofemoral ligament: Holds the kneecap on its outer side.
Keeps the kneecap tracking in its groove.
Tight lateral structures contribute to kneecap pain.
Lateral patellotibial ligament: Links the kneecap to the outer tibia.
Trapezius (lower): Keeps the shoulders down and relaxed.
Weakness lets the shoulders creep up.
Medial collateral ligament: Inner knee stability, especially if the knee drifts in.
MCL sprain from a blow to the outer knee or knee valgus.
Medial patellofemoral ligament: Main restraint against the kneecap slipping outward.
Medial patellotibial ligament: Links the kneecap to the inner tibia.
Trapezius (middle): Upper-back fatigue with a hunched posture.
Obturator internus: Steadies the hip joint in stance.
Palmaris longus: Bends the wrist and tightens the palm.
Patellar ligament: Connects the kneecap to the shin; transmits the quadriceps' pull.
Absorbs very high load at every landing.
Pectineus: Flexes the hip and pulls the thigh in.
Pectoralis major: Pulls the arm in front of the body and down.
Controls the forward part of the arm swing; it should not pull the arms across the body.
Tight chest muscles round the shoulders forward and spoil running posture.
Pectoralis minor: Pulls the shoulder blade forward and down.
Should stay relaxed so the shoulders stay open.
Piriformis: Rotates the thigh outward and steadies the hip.
Piriformis syndrome: buttock pain that can irritate the sciatic nerve.
Plantaris: Weakly helps point the foot and bend the knee.
Plantaris strain or rupture (sudden calf pain).
Popliteus: Unlocks the straight knee and rotates it.
Starts knee bending and steadies it, especially downhill.
Posterior cruciate ligament: Stops the shin sliding backward under the thigh.
Knee stability when the knee is bent.
PCL injury from a blow to the front of the shin.
Pronator teres: Turns the palm down and helps bend the elbow.
Golfer's elbow; can compress the median nerve.
Psoas major: The strongest hip flexor; also steadies the lumbar spine.
Swings the leg forward with every stride.
Tight hip flexors tilt the pelvis forward and load the low back.
Quadriceps tendon: Joins the quadriceps to the kneecap.
Transmits the knee-straightening force on landing and push-off.
Rectus femoris: Straightens the knee and flexes the hip.
Swings the leg through and controls knee bend at landing.
Rhomboid major: Pulls the shoulder blades together and up.
Rhomboid minor: Pulls the shoulder blades together and up.
Sartorius: Flexes, abducts and rotates the hip outward; bends the knee.
Helps lift and swing the leg.
Pain at its insertion below the inner knee (pes anserine).
Semimembranosus: Bends the knee and extends the hip.
Slows the leg in late swing and powers hip extension.
Semitendinosus: Bends the knee and extends the hip.
Slows the leg in late swing.
Soleus: Points the foot (with the knee bent or straight).
Takes the largest load of any muscle in running at push-off.
Subscapularis: Rotates the arm inward; rotator cuff.
Supinator: Can compress the radial nerve (forearm pain).
Supraspinatus: Starts lifting the arm out to the side; rotator cuff.
Keeps the shoulder centred during the arm swing.
The most commonly injured rotator cuff tendon.
Tensor fasciae latae: Flexes and abducts the hip and tensions the IT band.
Steadies the pelvis and knee in stance.
Tightness linked to IT band syndrome.
Teres major: Pulls the arm down, back and inward.
Teres minor: Rotates the arm outward; rotator cuff.
Tibialis anterior: Lifts the foot and supports the inner arch.
Lowers the foot gently after heel strike and clears the toes in swing.
Tibialis posterior: Points the foot, turns the sole inward and holds up the arch.
The main dynamic support of the arch at landing.
Medial shin splints; tendon dysfunction leads to a flat foot.
Trapezius (upper): Lifts the shoulder blades and supports the head.
Should stay relaxed: tension shrugs the shoulders up and wastes energy.
Neck and upper-back tension from a forward head or hunched, high shoulders.
Vastus intermedius: Absorbs landing and powers knee extension.
Vastus lateralis: The largest quadriceps: absorbs landing forces.
Imbalance with vastus medialis linked to kneecap pain.
Vastus medialis: Straightens the knee and steadies the kneecap.
Keeps the kneecap tracking straight at landing.
